evidence.text: walk
Phonosemantic compound. 辶 represents the meaning and 首 represents the sound.
所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道。

In the bronze inscriptions, a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l'uːʔ): semantic 行 (“street”) + phonetic 𩠐 (OC *hljuʔ, *hljus) + semantic 止 (“foot”). The 亍 on the right eventually disappeared, leading to the semantic components combining into 辵 in the seal script.
Possibly derived from 導 (OC *duːs, “to go along, to bring along, to conduct”):
* > "to explain" > "to talk about", and
* > "road, way".
Possibly cognate with Proto-Hmong-Mien *kləuX (“road, way”) (> White Hmong kev (“road”)). See also 首 (OC *hljuʔ, *hljus).
所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道。

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: 道 entry; original definition, component account, extended meanings
evidence.text: The entry defines 道 as a way people travel, analyzes it as 辵 plus 𩠐/首, and gives “one-way access” as a definition. Duan Yucai says 首 also supplies sound, identifies the pronunciation as 徒皓切, and reports extensions to 道理 and 引道. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graphic analysis or the chronology of those extensions.
evidence.title: 說文解字「道」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 道: Shuowen forms, component spelling, pronunciation and senses
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the Shuowen definition and its analysis as 辵 plus 首, records the older graph 𡬹 as 首 plus 寸, and gives Mandarin dào. It documents a broad set of variant graphs. Its senses include road or route, journey, guiding, method or principle, and later philosophical, verbal and classifier uses; the senses and cited literary examples do not by themselves establish a chronological semantic chain.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》 entry A04159 道

evidence.field: 道: formation, component readings, historical pronunciation and graphic timeline
evidence.text: The page analyzes 辶 as the meaning component and 首 as the sound component; it reports Mandarin readings chuò and shǒu for those components and dào for 道, and gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese forms 道 *lˤuʔ-s / *[kə.l]ˤuʔ and 首 *l̥uʔ / *l̥uʔ-s, followed by Middle Chinese dawH/dawX for 道. It labels its displayed bronze form Early Western Zhou (~1000 BCE), seal form Shuowen (~100 CE), and clerical form Eastern Han (25–220 CE). These are the page's assertions; its seal/bronze image content was not independently visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 道 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: ECNU Journal of Chinese Language and Literature Education
evidence.text: The article states that, in currently known materials, 道 first appears in bronze inscriptions and has not been found in oracle-bone inscriptions. It interprets the original sense as road and repeats the Shuowen analysis. The broad claim is useful but the opened passage gives no specific inscription, vessel, or dated occurrence; thus the earliest individual attestation remains unverified here.
evidence.title: 《文》与《道》在语文教育中的探讨

evidence.source: Japanese Wiktionary, 道 entry and cited bibliography
evidence.field: 字源, competing analyses and source references
evidence.text: The entry identifies 辵 as semantic and 首 as phonetic, with cited Old Chinese forms 道 /*lˤuʔ/ and 首 /*LU/ in the referenced analysis. It reports an alternative interpretation of bronze forms as a head carried for ritual purification, then cites scholarship arguing against it: 首 has phonetic-series behavior and variant forms reportedly substitute 舀; the entry says evidence for that ritual-origin claim is lacking. The listed bibliography includes paleographic works by Zhang Shichao et al., Huang Dekuan et al., Liu Zhao, and Yan Yiping. This is a report of disputed scholarship, not a direct examination of those books.

evidence.field: 道 and 導 phonetic-series relationship
evidence.text: The page lists 導 as both a meaning and sound component use associated with 道, and gives distinct Old Chinese forms for 道’s “show the way” and “way” readings. This establishes that a derivational or cognate relationship between the verbs and road sense cannot be inferred from the graph alone; the dossier's proposed derivation from 導 remains unverified by the inspected evidence.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No specific dated bronze artifact or primary inscription bearing 道 was inspected. The ECNU article's claim that the graph is absent from oracle-bone inscriptions and first appears in bronze inscriptions therefore remains a reported secondary claim, not a verified earliest attestation.
No glyph image was visually inspected. The proposed bronze graphic sequence, including the dossier's account of 行, 止, and loss or merger of 亍 into 辵, is not independently confirmed here.

The sound role of 首 is supported by Shuowen's explicit 声 statement in Duan Yucai and the cited phonological comparisons, but modern Mandarin readings are not close: 道 dào versus 首 shǒu. Dong supplies Baxter–Sagart reconstructions; Japanese Wiktionary supplies a different notation /*lˤuʔ/ and /*LU/. Their differing forms and variant readings should not be collapsed across reconstruction systems.

The actual spoken-word chronology is not established from dictionary gloss order. Sources report road/route and later extended senses, but dated earliest attestations for senses such as method, principle, guiding, and speaking were not individually established.

The derivation of the road sense from 導, the proposed Proto-Hmong-Mien cognacy, and any borrowing direction remain unsettled in the inspected material. No independent source-word or borrowing case was verified.
The alleged ritual interpretation involving a carried head is disputed and lacks direct evidence in the accessed sources. No evidence here establishes an alternative ritual object or name.
The bronze-form relationship to 𡬹 (首 plus 寸) is recorded as a Shuowen ancient form; available evidence does not establish whether it is an ancestor, a variant, or another historical relation.

No identified physical bronze artifact bearing 道 was inspected, and no individually dated earliest bronze occurrence was verified. The claim that 道 is absent from oracle-bone inscriptions and first appears in bronzes remains a secondary report.

Commons candidates are modern digital vector redrawings, not artifact photographs. The web tool did not render the SVG pixels, so the proposed captions are based on the files' inspected descriptions and provenance only.

No direct inscription evidence was inspected to confirm the reported 行/止/亍 components, loss or fusion of 亍, or the graphic relation of the bronze and seal forms. The seal-style reconstruction is compatible with Shuowen's 辵+𩠐 account, but not proof of bronze morphology.
Shuowen's 𡬹 (首+寸) is called a 古文 form, but the evidence inspected does not establish whether it is an ancestor, descendant, or nonchronological variant relative to 道.

首 is independently attested with a head sense in early literary material, but the derivation of 道's phonetic role rests on lexicographic and reconstruction sources; the proposed cognacy/derivation with 導 and Proto-Hmong-Mien remains unverified. The character's sound-component role does not require identifying an original object depicted by 首.

Road/way use occurs in the transmitted Classic of Poetry 大東, but the exact composition date and earliest attestation cannot be fixed from the inspected page. Extensions such as method, principle, guiding, speaking, philosophical Dao, and classifier uses are listed in later dictionaries but their chronological semantic links are not established here.

The Dao De Jing and Chinese Text Project results could not be inspected past search output because the page requests returned 403. Their search snippets are not used as inspected evidence or firm date claims. No evidence supports a whole-graph loan analysis for 道 in this pass.

items.alt: Black bronze-script-style 道 glyph with a dense central form and strokes extending to the left and right, on a white field.
items.selection_reason: Its distinctive graphic form helps illustrate the reported bronze-script evidence, while the caption avoids treating the redraw as an artifact or asserting an unverified component analysis.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style, conventionally associated with the Han Shuowen tradition; SVG upload in 2006 does not date the glyph itself.

items.alt: Black seal-script-style 道 glyph with a tall, rounded central form and enclosing strokes, on a white field.
items.selection_reason: It provides a useful comparison with the bronze-style rendering and illustrates the received Shuowen analysis, without implying that the two images establish a direct chronological sequence.
items.rights: Wikimedia Commons description declares the SVG public domain, including a public-domain release of the rendering.

limitations.text: Both images are modern digital redrawings, not photographs or facsimiles of identified ancient artifacts. No specific bronze inscription, date, or earliest attestation is established here; the report that 道 first appears in bronze inscriptions remains unverified at the level of an individual object.

The bronze form’s graphic parts and their proposed relation to 行, 止, and 辵 are not confirmed by an inspected inscription. Shuowen’s 辵-plus-𩠐 analysis is a historical dictionary account, not independent proof of the bronze form’s morphology.
